content.body: Have you ever wondered how to efficiently find all subarrays that sum to a specific number? In this lesson, we'll learn a clever technique using a hash map to solve this common problem. You'll discover how remembering what you've already seen can dramatically improve your algorithm's speed.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
1. Explain why brute force checking every subarray is inefficient
2. Apply the concept of prefix sums to understand subarray sums
3. Implement a hash map solution to count subarrays summing to K
4. Determine what to store as keys and values in your lookup structure
5. Decide when to check the structure versus when to add to it
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: In the array [1, 2, 3], which subarrays sum to 3?
content.successMessage: Great! You found [1, 2] and [3] as subarrays that sum to 3.

content.title: Try a bigger array
content.successMessage: Well done! You found [2, 1, 3] and [4, 2] as subarrays that sum to 6.

content.successMessage: Excellent! You found several subarrays like [1, -1, 1, 1] and [1, 1] that sum to 2.

content.body: What you just did was brute force: you checked every possible subarray by considering all starting and ending points. For each subarray, you calculated the sum from scratch. This works for small arrays but becomes very slow as arrays grow larger.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the array has 10,000 elements, checking every possible subarray means checking millions of combinations. Each subarray sum calculation can be expensive too. We need a smarter method that avoids re-scanning and re-calculating. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: The key insight is to remember what we have already seen. Instead of recalculating sums for every subarray, we can keep track of prefix sums (running totals) as we move through the array. Then we use a lookup structure (like a JavaScript object or Map) to remember which prefix sums we've encountered and how many times we've seen them.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like a notebook where we write down every running total we've calculated so far. When we get a new running total, we check our notebook to see if we've previously had a running total that's exactly K less than our current one. If we have, we know we've found subarrays that sum to K.

content.body: We'll use a single pass through the array while maintaining a running total (prefix sum). At each step, we check if we've previously seen a prefix sum that's exactly (current prefix sum - K). If yes, we add to our count. Then we record the current prefix sum in our lookup structure.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Initialize a count variable to 0 and a prefix sum variable to 0
2. Create a lookup object/map and initialize it with {0:1} (a prefix sum of 0 occurs once before we start)
3. Loop through each number in the array:
   a. Add the current number to the prefix sum
   b. Calculate needed = prefix sum - K
   c. If needed exists in the lookup, add its value to count
   d. Add/update the current prefix sum in the lookup
4. Return the count

content.body:
Congratulations! You've implemented an efficient solution to count subarrays summing to K. Remember these key points:

1. We store prefix sums as keys in our lookup structure and their frequencies as values
2. We check the structure BEFORE adding the current prefix sum (to avoid counting the current element as matching itself)
3. The initial {0: 1} in the map handles subarrays starting from index 0
4. This approach transforms an O(n²) brute force solution into an O(n) efficient algorithm

This 'remember what we've already seen' pattern with hash maps is powerful for many array problems!
